Farmers Solar Up

By: Mart-Marie Faure | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Unreliable power supply and above-inflation rising costs in electricity has prompted some farmers to solar up. But it has been a bumpy and costly journey.

Unique Selling Point:
Many farmers are fed-up with rising costs of electricity and an unreliably supply from an ailing Eskom. What needed to be done was to install solar farms in order to generate their own power. Some farmers invested more than R20 000000 to install solar farms. They are able to generate up to 1MW. These units are Grid Access units which means that they are linked to the Eskom grid, allowing farmers to generate not only their own power but to also pump into the national grid, making them IPP's. Before 2014 Eskom put a license structure in place. But from 2014 to 2017, during the Zuma years government became reluctant to support IPP's and by 2017 solar farms generating 1MW and less were instructed to register with NERSA. NERSA had no plan or structures in place to run this registration process and some farmers had to cover the cost of their installation for more than 4 years some at a cost of R6 000.per day. Agri SA claims that if NERSA had their house in order sooner Level 1 load shedding could have been prevented. NERSA claimed that they needed to establish a suitable registration tariff. This took months and recently they announced that a mere R200.00 would be suitable, however they still didn't have an administrative n process in place. in 2017 NERSA stopped the registration process in order to get the administrative process going leaving applications in limbo. Applications for 14000 MW in solar farms have been gathering dust at NERSA. The delay is costing some farmers between R3000 and 6000 per day. This includes the farm, Sonvrugt, a Black Economic Empowerment farm near Kakamas.

Press Release:


Solar Farmers in Limbo
As colder weather sets in, Eskom says electricity demand will spike, and the risk of load shedding returns. Carte Blanche meets farmers who have installed enough solar to power their own operations and feed back into the national grid to relieve the pressure. We sit down with the National Energy Regulator of South Africa to examine how the growing number of independent power producers is being regulated.
Producer: Mart-Marie Faure
Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Unreliable power supply and above-inflation rising costs in electricity has prompted some farmers to solar up. But it has been a bumpy and costly journey.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Many farmers are fed-up with rising costs of electricity and an unreliably supply from an ailing Eskom. What needed to be done was to install solar farms in order to generate their own power. Some farmers invested more than R20 000000 to install solar farms. They are able to generate up to 1MW. These units are Grid Access units which means that they are linked to the Eskom grid, allowing farmers to generate not only their own power but to also pump into the national grid, making them IPP's. Before 2014 Eskom put a license structure in place. But from 2014 to 2017, during the Zuma years government became reluctant to support IPP's and by 2017 solar farms generating 1MW and less were instructed to register with NERSA. NERSA had no plan or structures in place to run this registration process and some farmers had to cover the cost of their installation for more than 4 years some at a cost of R6 000.per day. Agri SA claims that if NERSA had their house in order sooner Level 1 load shedding could have been prevented. NERSA claimed that they needed to establish a suitable registration tariff. This took months and recently they announced that a mere R200.00 would be suitable, however they still didn't have an administrative n process in place. in 2017 NERSA stopped the registration process in order to get the administrative process going leaving applications in limbo. Applications for 14000 MW in solar farms have been gathering dust at NERSA. The delay is costing some farmers between R3000 and 6000 per day. This includes the farm, Sonvrugt, a Black Economic Empowerment farm near Kakamas.
